summary: Defines an initial use of IP and ARP in an ATM network set up as a Logical IP Subnetwork, how IP packets and address lookup work over ATM. It was replaced by RFC 2225.

eli5.summary: ATM is a different kind of network. This memo shows how to run Internet addressing on top of it as if it were a regular local network.

subtitle: Running IP networks over ATM as if it were Ethernet.

tldr.problem: ATM networks are fundamentally different from Ethernet LANs, but early deployment needed a way to run the familiar IP and ARP protocols over ATM with minimal changes to existing IP routing.
tldr.mechanism: The Logical IP Subnetwork (LIS) treats each ATM network like a traditional subnet. Hosts resolve IP addresses to ATM addresses using ATMARP (ARP adapted for ATM), and communicate directly via virtual circuits within the same subnet.
tldr.outcome: This allowed early ATM networks to be deployed as drop-in replacements for Ethernet segments. The approach was practical but had limitations; it was later superseded by RFC 2225.

today: RFC 1577 specified how to run IP and ARP over ATM networks using the Logical IP Subnetwork model. It was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 2225.

sections.title: Introduction and Goal
sections.content:
The goal of this RFC is to define how to transmit IP datagrams and ARP requests over Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) networks. ATM is a switching technology fundamentally different from Ethernet: it uses virtual circuits and small fixed-size cells instead of frames, and requires explicit addressing and connection setup.

This memo defines a classical model: treating an ATM network as a direct replacement for a local area network segment. IP routing stays the same, hosts communicate within the same subnet via virtual circuits (VCs), and address resolution uses an adapted form of ARP called ATMARP. This approach is practical for early ATM deployments but does not address future globally-connected ATM networks.
sections.eli5: ATM networks work differently from regular networks. This explains how to make IP work on top of ATM without changing how routers think.

sections.title: The Logical IP Subnetwork (LIS)
sections.content:
In the LIS model, an administrator configures a group of IP hosts and routers to form a single logical IP subnet over shared ATM infrastructure. All members of the LIS:

  • Share the same IP network/subnet number and address mask.
  • Connect directly to the ATM network.
  • Communicate with each other directly via virtual circuits.
  • Access hosts outside the LIS through an IP router.

The key insight is that each LIS operates independently. Multiple LISs can exist on the same ATM network, but hosts in different LISs must use a router to communicate, even if a direct ATM path is available. This preserves the boundary semantics of IP subnetting.

An ATM network can replace both local area network segments (connecting hosts) and point-to-point links (connecting routers). Importantly, the network uses AAL5 (ATM Adaptation Layer 5) for encapsulation, which provides packets up to 64KB in size over ATM's small 53-byte cells.
sections.eli5: A group of computers and routers share the same IP address block and connect via ATM like they would on Ethernet. To talk to computers on other subnets, data goes through a router.

sections.title: Address Resolution: ATMARP and InATMARP
sections.content:
IP hosts need to resolve IP addresses to ATM addresses, just as they resolve IP to Ethernet addresses using ARP. The solution is ATMARP (ATM Address Resolution Protocol), which is ARP with extensions for ATM's longer address format.

ATM addresses come in two forms: NSAPA (an identifier similar to OSI addresses) and E.164 (a public network identifier). Each IP station must know its own IP address and its ATM address(es).

InATMARP (Inverse ATMARP) is used to do the reverse: learn an IP address from an ATM address. With Permanent Virtual Circuits (PVCs), which are manually configured, InATMARP is used to query the remote end and populate the ARP table. With Switched Virtual Circuits (SVCs), which are set up dynamically, an ATMARP Server holds the authoritative mapping and replies to ATMARP requests from clients.

ATMARP and InATMARP packets are encapsulated in AAL5 using the same LLC/SNAP format as IP datagrams (8 octets of header, then the protocol data). The ATMARP hardware type is 19, and the operation codes are REQUEST, REPLY, InARP_REQUEST, InARP_REPLY, and ARP_NAK (a new code meaning the address was not found).
sections.eli5: To send data to another computer, you need to know its ATM address. ATMARP is like Ethernet's address lookup, but works over ATM. An ATMARP server keeps a phone book for switched circuits.

sections.title: Operating with PVCs and SVCs
sections.content:
With Permanent Virtual Circuits (PVCs), connections are manually set up beforehand. An IP station is configured with the PVCs it has. When the station wants to talk to a peer, it uses the appropriate PVC and sends an InATMARP request to learn the remote IP address. The peer replies with InATMARP and both sides can exchange IP traffic.

With Switched Virtual Circuits (SVCs), connections are set up dynamically. All IP stations in a LIS must be configured with the ATM address of a single ATMARP Server. When a client needs to send to a destination:

  • The client sets up an SVC to the ATMARP Server.
  • The server receives the connection and sends an InATMARP request to learn the client's IP address.
  • The client replies with InATMARP, and the server stores the mapping.
  • When the client sends ATMARP requests to resolve other IP addresses, the server looks them up in its table and replies with ATMARP responses or ARP_NAK if not found.

The ATMARP server also supports table aging: entries are valid for at least 20 minutes on the server and at most 15 minutes on clients. The server probes entries before aging them out to keep active peers registered.
sections.eli5: For fixed connections, both sides send a special message to learn each other's address. For dynamic connections, a central ATMARP server keeps track of who is who and answers address lookup requests.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 1577 was a Proposed Standard for classical IP and ARP over ATM. The approach worked for early ATM deployments but was limited by the LIS model, which could not scale to globally-connected ATM networks. It has been obsoleted by RFC 2225, which refines and extends the approach.
sections.eli5: This was an initial attempt to use ATM for IP networks. Later versions improved on the design.
